q-79818.name: Question 1
q-79818.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y={e}^{x},\,x>0
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
q-79818.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ and $Q(x)={e}^{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\cdot y) & =x\cdot {e}^{x} \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =x{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx) & =x{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

q-335274.name: Question 2
q-335274.problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy=\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
q-335274.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=2x$ and $Q(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2x\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+2x{e}^{{x}^{2}}\cdot y & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}}) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function y=y(x): dydx+2xy=sin⁡x Write the equation in the form ddx(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x), where I(x) is an integrating factor.

a
ddx(yx2)=x2sin⁡x
b
ddx(yln⁡|2x|)=ln⁡|2x|sin⁡x
c
ddx(yex2)=ex2sin⁡x
d
ddx(y⋅2x)=2xsin⁡x
e
ddx(ye2x)=e2xsin⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

This equation is in the standard form dydx+P(x)y=Q(x) with P(x)=2x and Q(x)=sin⁡x. We proceed to find an integrating factor I(x) using the definition: I(x)=e∫P(x)dx=e∫2xdx=ex2

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by I(x)=ex2 as follows: ex2⋅(dydx+2xy)=ex2⋅sin⁡xex2⋅dydx+2xex2⋅y=ex2sin⁡x

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as ddx(y⋅I(x)): ddx(yex2)=ex2sin⁡x

q-339139.name: Question 3
q-339139.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{4}{x}y=5,\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below:

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
q-339139.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{4}{x}$ and $Q(x)=5.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (4/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4})} \\  & ={x}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{4}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{4}{x}y) & ={x}^{4}\cdot 5 \\ {x}^{4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4{x}^{3}y & =5{x}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{4})\,dx & =\int 5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{4} & ={x}^{5}+C \\ y & =x+\frac{C}{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-335412.name: Question 4
q-335412.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
q-335412.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$

$$

q-335808.name: Question 5
q-335808.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}\cdot y=x,\,y(0)=1
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The solution to the initial value problem is $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
q-335808.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{x}{2}$ and $Q(x)=x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (x/2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot x \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{x}{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\cdot y & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}) & =x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4})\text{d}x & =\int x{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =\int 2{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{2}/4} & =2{e}^{{x}^{2}/4}+C \\ y & =2+C{e}^{-{x}^{2}/4}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =2+C{e}^{-{0}^{2}/4} \\ 1 & =2+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2-{e}^{-{x}^{2}/4}.
$$

q-335830.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(0)=4
$$

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

q-335830.worked_solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=-2$ and $Q(x)={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{-2x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y) & ={e}^{-2x}\cdot {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {e}^{-2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2{e}^{-2x}\cdot y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-2x}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-2x})\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-2x} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & ={e}^{2x}(C-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0)=4$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={e}^{2(0)}(C-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\ 4 & =C-1 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$

EXPLANATION

This equation is in the standard form dydx+P(x)y=Q(x), with P(x)=−2 and Q(x)=e2xsin⁡(x).

We compute an integrating factor using the definition: I(x)=e∫P(x)dx=e∫(−2)dx=e−2x

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by I(x)=e−2x yields e−2x⋅(dydx−2y)=e−2x⋅e2xsin⁡xe−2x⋅dydx−2e−2x⋅y=sin⁡xddx(ye−2x)=sin⁡x.

Now, we integrate with respect to x: ∫ddx(ye−2x)dx=∫sin⁡xdxye−2x=−cos⁡x+Cy=e2x(C−cos⁡x)

This is the general solution. To find the value of C corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition y(0)=4 as follows: y(0)=e2(0)(C−cos⁡0)4=C−1C=5

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y=e2x(5−cos⁡x).
